periods.activity_title: From Freehand to Compass: Drawing a Circle

textbook_items_in_class.description: Students mark a point P, then use a compass set to 4 cm to trace all points 4 cm from P, discovering that the resulting curve is a circle with centre P and radius 4 cm.

time_bands.activity: Students attempt to draw a circle freehand on plain paper, then compare results to discuss what makes a circle precise. The class arrives at the idea that every point on a circle must be exactly the same distance from a fixed centre.

Activity (compass exploration), section 8.1 p.188 ("Students mark a point P, then use a compass set to 4 cm to trace all points….") — each student marks a point P, sets the compass to 4 cm, and traces the full curve, confirming that the resulting shape is a circle with centre P and radius 4 cm.

Students vary the compass opening to 3 cm and 5 cm, draw two more circles from the same centre P, and record what changes (size) and what stays the same (all points equidistant from P). Pairs share observations aloud.

Class discussion: students articulate in their own words what 'radius' means and why the compass guarantees equal distance. Teacher asks: 'Can you draw a circle without lifting the compass point from P?' to consolidate the definition.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who reposition the compass pivot while drawing — this breaks the equidistance guarantee and produces a spiral rather than a circle; a quick demonstration of keeping the needle fixed corrects this. Students who finish quickly can try estimating the radius needed to draw a circle that just fits inside a 6 cm square drawn on the same sheet.

periods.activity_title: Building the Wavy Wave with Half-Circles

textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a wavy wave on a baseline AB of 8 cm by drawing successive half-circles: first half-circle has radius 2 cm centred at the midpoint X of AX = 4 cm, with each subsequent wave mirroring the first.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 8.1 p.191
textbook_items_in_class.description: What radius should be taken in the compass to draw the first half-circle of the Wavy Wave? What should be the length of AX?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 8.1 p.191
textbook_items_in_class.description: Take a central baseline of a different length and draw the wavy wave on it.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 8.1 p.191
homework.description: Try to recreate the figure where the waves are smaller than a half-circle (as in the neck of 'A Person'). The challenge is to get both waves identical.

time_bands.activity: Teacher walks through Construct (Wavy Wave), section 8.1 p.191 ("Construct a wavy wave on a baseline AB of 8 cm by drawing successive half-circles…."), drawing the first half-circle on the board and inviting students to predict where the second centre goes before drawing it.

Students construct their own wavy wave, then answer Figure it Out Q1, section 8.1 p.191 ("What radius should be taken in the compass to draw the first half-circle….") by measuring their own drawing and reasoning about the relationship between baseline length and radius.

Figure it Out Q2, section 8.1 p.191 ("Take a central baseline of a different length and draw the wavy wave….") — students choose a different baseline length, plan the number and size of half-circles, and construct the new wave, making their planning decisions explicit in a brief written note beside the figure.
Pairs compare waves with different baselines and discuss: 'What stays the same about how you place each centre?' Class arrives at the rule: each centre is the midpoint of its segment of the baseline.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is placing the second half-circle centre at the same point as the first rather than shifting along the baseline; circulating during construction and asking 'Where is your next centre?' surfaces this quickly. Students who complete Q2 early can attempt Figure it Out Q3, section 8.1 p.191, which asks for waves smaller than a half-circle.

periods.activity_title: Naming, Rotating, and Recognising Squares and Rectangles

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q (naming square), section 8.2 p.193
textbook_items_in_class.description: Identify which of the four given names (PQSR, SPQR, RSPQ, QRSP) is not a valid name for the given square.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 8.2 p.194
textbook_items_in_class.description: Identify if any of the four given figures (A, B, C, D) are squares using measurements; then reason whether sides and angles can be determined from dot-grid position alone.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 8.2 p.194
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw at least 3 rotated squares and rectangles on a dot grid with corners on dots; verify they satisfy the respective properties.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a rectangle ABCD on the board, labels its corners, and asks students to list all valid names by tracing around the figure. The class identifies the two properties R1 (opposite sides equal) and R2 (all angles 90°) through measurement of the drawn figure, then repeats for a square to identify S1 and S2.

Figure it Out Q (naming square), section 8.2 p.193 ("Identify which of the four given names (PQSR, SPQR, RSPQ, QRSP) is not valid….") — students work individually, then pairs compare and explain their reasoning for rejecting one name.

Figure it Out Q2, section 8.2 p.194 ("Identify if any of the four given figures are squares using measurements….") — students measure sides and angles on the dot-grid figures and record whether each figure qualifies, explicitly noting which property is violated when it does not.

Figure it Out Q3, section 8.2 p.194 ("Draw at least 3 rotated squares and rectangles on a dot grid….") — students draw rotated figures on dot paper and verify properties by measurement, building the understanding that rotation preserves side lengths and angles.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently believe that a tilted square 'becomes a diamond' and lose confidence identifying it as a square; measuring all four sides and all four angles on their own rotated figure is the most effective correction. Figure it Out Q1, section 8.2 p.194 (drawing a rectangle-and-four-squares configuration) can serve as a self-study pointer for students who want extra practice with the properties.

periods.activity_title: Constructing a Square Step by Step

textbook_items_in_class.description: Six-step construction of square PQRS with side 6 cm: draw PQ; raise perpendicular at P; mark S at 6 cm on perpendicular; raise perpendicular at Q; use compass to mark R at 6 cm from both S and Q; join to complete.
Draw a rectangle with sides 4 cm and 6 cm and verify it satisfies both rectangle properties.

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: 'Given that a square has all sides equal and all angles 90°, which of these two properties should we use first when constructing one, and why?' Students briefly discuss in pairs to frame the deductive approach.

Construct (Square PQRS, 6 cm), section 8.3 p.195 ("Six-step construction of square PQRS with side 6 cm: draw PQ; raise perpendicular at P….") — teacher leads each step on the board while students follow simultaneously at their desks, pausing after each step to confirm both properties are being maintained.

Construct Q1, section 8.3 p.197 ("Draw a rectangle with sides 4 cm and 6 cm and verify it satisfies both rectangle properties….") — students apply the same perpendicular-raising technique independently to construct a rectangle, then measure all sides and angles to verify R1 and R2.
Quick whole-class check: teacher calls on two students to state the two rectangle properties they verified, embedding the formal vocabulary R1 and R2 in spoken language.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error in this construction is a slightly inaccurate perpendicular — a gap of even 1–2 mm at the compass pivot produces a visibly non-right angle; encourage students to check with a protractor after construction and diagnose which step introduced the error. Construct Q2, section 8.3 p.197 (2 cm × 10 cm rectangle) is a useful self-study item for students who want a second independent construction before the next challenge.

periods.activity_title: Rectangles, Right Angles, and the Impossible Figure

textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw a rectangle with sides 2 cm and 10 cm and verify it satisfies both rectangle properties.
Is it possible to construct a 4-sided figure in which all angles are 90° but opposite sides are not equal? Reason and answer.

time_bands.activity: Construct Q2, section 8.3 p.197 ("Draw a rectangle with sides 2 cm and 10 cm and verify it satisfies both rectangle properties….") — students construct the narrow rectangle independently using the perpendicular method from the previous construction, then verify both properties and note any construction challenges introduced by the extreme aspect ratio.

Try This Q3, section 8.3 p.197 ("Is it possible to construct a 4-sided figure in which all angles are 90° but opposite sides are not equal?….") — students attempt to draw such a figure on plain paper, discuss in pairs what happens to the fourth side when three 90° angles are fixed, and write a short justification.

Whole-class discussion: pairs share their reasoning. Teacher asks 'If you fix three corners at 90°, is the fourth corner's angle a free choice?' leading to the conclusion that all four 90° angles force opposite sides to be equal, making the figure a rectangle.

periods.teacher_notes: For Try This Q3, students often try to make a figure with one pair of sides unequal and are surprised when the fourth angle refuses to close at 90°; letting them experience this failure physically — attempting the construction and observing the gap — is more convincing than a verbal proof. Watch for students who confuse 'all angles 90°' with 'all sides equal', which is the square condition, not what this problem is asking.

periods.activity_title: Closest and Farthest: Tracking XY Across a Rectangle

textbook_items_in_class.description: In rectangle ABCD (AB = 7 cm, BC = 4 cm), predict and verify by measurement: at which positions of X on AD and Y on BC are they closest and farthest apart?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q (table), section 8.4 p.198
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill a table recording the length XY for at least three different positions of X and Y (given distances from A and B respectively).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q (same-distance), section 8.4 p.199
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill the table for cases where X and Y are equidistant from A and B respectively; observe the resulting length XY and the shape of ABYX.

time_bands.activity: Students construct rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm, BC = 4 cm using the ruler and compass method. Teacher marks a point X on AD and Y on BC and poses the Math Talk question from Math Talk, section 8.4 p.198 ("At which positions of X on AD and Y on BC are they closest and farthest apart?….") — students write individual predictions before any measurement.

Figure it Out Q (table), section 8.4 p.198 ("Fill a table recording the length XY for at least three different positions….") — student pairs mark three different X, Y positions, measure XY each time, and record in the table, looking for a pattern in when XY is shortest.

Figure it Out Q (same-distance), section 8.4 p.199 ("Fill the table for cases where X and Y are equidistant from A and B respectively….") — students systematically place X and Y at equal distances from A and B, measure XY, and notice that XY equals AB and ABYX forms a rectangle.

Class discussion: 'Why does XY equal AB when X and Y are equidistant from A and B?' Students use the rectangle property R1 to reason that ABYX has opposite sides equal and all angles 90°, confirming it is a rectangle.

periods.teacher_notes: Students are often surprised that XY is shortest when X and Y are at equal distances from their respective corners, not when they are at the nearest ends; encouraging predictions before measurement makes this discovery more vivid. A common reasoning error is assuming XY must be shorter than AB because it 'cuts across'; the table data directly challenges this misconception.

periods.activity_title: Farthest Distance and the Diagonal Connection

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q (farthest distance), section 8.4 p.199
textbook_items_in_class.description: How does the farthest distance between X and Y compare with the length of diagonal AC or BD?
Construct a rectangle that can be divided into two identical squares.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q (farthest distance), section 8.4 p.199 ("How does the farthest distance between X and Y compare with the length of diagonal AC or BD?….") — students measure the diagonal of their rectangle ABCD and compare with the maximum XY value found in their table, recording the comparison and articulating the relationship in words.

Teacher demonstrates the compass length-transfer technique: opening the compass to span a segment and swinging an arc to reproduce that length at a new position without reading a ruler measurement. Students practise transferring a 5 cm segment to a new location on their paper using compass only.

Explore (two squares), section 8.4 p.199 ("Construct a rectangle that can be divided into two identical squares….") — students plan the required relationship between length and breadth (length = twice breadth), choose a breadth, use the compass-transfer technique to mark the length, then construct the rectangle and verify it divides into two squares.
Pairs share their chosen measurements and confirm the 2:1 ratio, reinforcing that the compass-transfer technique works for any chosen breadth without needing to pre-measure the length on a ruler.

periods.teacher_notes: The compass-transfer technique is new to most students at this stage; the key error is lifting and re-setting the compass between spanning and swinging — emphasise that the opening must not change. Having established that the farthest distance equals the diagonal through measurement, students are well placed to appreciate why the rectangle-into-two-squares construction relies on an exact ratio rather than approximation.

periods.activity_title: Breaking Rectangles: Two and Three Identical Squares

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Construct (Breaking Rectangles — two squares), section 8.4 p.200
textbook_items_in_class.description: Plan and construct a rectangle divisible into two identical squares: set AF to any chosen length, transfer AF using compass to mark B at AB = AF, raise perpendicular at B, mark C at BC = AF, join to complete rectangle ACDF.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Construct (Breaking Rectangles — three squares), section 8.4 p.199
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a rectangle that can be divided into three identical squares.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (sides not divisible), section 8.4 p.201
textbook_items_in_class.description: Give the side lengths of a rectangle that cannot be divided into (a) two identical squares; (b) three identical squares.

time_bands.activity: Construct (Breaking Rectangles — two squares), section 8.4 p.200 ("Plan and construct a rectangle divisible into two identical squares: set AF to any chosen length, transfer AF using compass….") — teacher walks through the full construction on the board, narrating each compass-transfer step, while students follow on paper.

Construct (Breaking Rectangles — three squares), section 8.4 p.199 ("Construct a rectangle that can be divided into three identical squares….") — students plan the required length-to-breadth ratio (3:1), choose measurements, construct using compass transfer, and verify by dividing the finished rectangle into three equal squares.

Figure it Out (sides not divisible), section 8.4 p.201 ("Give the side lengths of a rectangle that cannot be divided into (a) two identical squares; (b) three identical squares….") — students reason about divisibility conditions and write at least two side-length pairs for each case, explaining why the ratio fails.

Brief share-out: students state one pair of sides that fails for two-square division and explain the rule in their own words — reinforcing that 'length must be exactly twice the breadth' is necessary, not just convenient.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often try to use the ruler to measure the length as twice the breadth rather than using compass transfer; redirect by asking 'Can you get the same result if your breadth was an awkward number like 3.7 cm?' to motivate the compass method. Watch for the misconception that any rectangle with a 'nice' length can be split into identical squares — the divisibility condition is precise.

periods.activity_title: Construction Challenges: Squares Inside Rectangles

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Construct Q1 (Square within Rectangle), section 8.4 p.201
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a rectangle of sides 8 cm and 4 cm, then construct a square inside it such that the centre of the square coincides with the centre of the rectangle.
Construct three aligned falling squares of side 4 cm each, then replicate the pattern with squares of sides 3 cm, 5 cm, and 7 cm.

time_bands.activity: Students make a rough sketch of the Square within a Rectangle figure, labelling the known dimensions (8 cm × 4 cm rectangle) and estimating the required square side, reasoning from symmetry that the square's side must equal the shorter side of the rectangle.

Construct Q1 (Square within Rectangle), section 8.4 p.201 ("Construct a rectangle of sides 8 cm and 4 cm, then construct a square inside it such that the centre of the square coincides….") — students construct the rectangle, find its centre using diagonal intersection, then use compass and ruler to inscribe the square symmetrically, checking that all four inner corners lie on the rectangle's sides.

Construct Q2 (Falling Squares), section 8.4 p.202 ("Construct three aligned falling squares of side 4 cm each, then replicate the pattern with squares of sides 3 cm, 5 cm, and 7 cm….") — students plan the alignment of the three squares on a rough sketch, then execute the construction, verifying that each square satisfies S1 and S2.
Quick peer-check: students exchange books and verify one square in their partner's Falling Squares construction by measuring two sides and one angle, giving oral feedback.

periods.teacher_notes: For the Square within a Rectangle, students sometimes attempt to centre the square by eye rather than by locating the intersection of the diagonals; insisting on the construction method builds the habit of using geometric properties rather than estimation. In Falling Squares, watch for misalignment caused by not maintaining perpendicularity when shifting to the next square.

periods.activity_title: Shadings, Holes, and Curves: Creative Construction Challenges

textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a shading figure (a square containing smaller squares) with measurements of own choice.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Construct Q4 (Square with a Hole), section 8.4 p.202
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a square with a circular hole at its centre; the hole's centre coincides with the square's centre.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Construct Q5 (Square with More Holes), section 8.4 p.202
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a square with multiple circular holes.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Try This (Square with Curves), section 8.4 p.202
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a square of side 8 cm with four arcs bulging uniformly from each side; determine the correct centre placement for the compass to produce symmetric arcs.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents all four challenges — Shadings, Square with a Hole, Square with More Holes, and Square with Curves — as a gallery of target figures. Students select which challenge to begin with and make a rough planning sketch, deciding their own measurements and compass placements before picking up instruments.

Students work on their chosen challenges: Construct Q3 (Shadings), section 8.4 p.202 ("Construct a shading figure — a square containing smaller squares…."), Construct Q4 (Square with a Hole), section 8.4 p.202 ("Construct a square with a circular hole at its centre…."), and Construct Q5 (Square with More Holes), section 8.4 p.202 ("Construct a square with multiple circular holes…."), progressing through challenges as they complete each. Teacher circulates, prompting with 'How did you decide where to place that centre?'

Try This (Square with Curves), section 8.4 p.202 ("Construct a square of side 8 cm with four arcs bulging uniformly from each side; determine the correct centre placement….") — students attempt this extension challenge, reasoning about symmetry to place compass centres at the midpoints of opposite sides.
Students share one decision they made about compass placement and explain why they chose that centre, connecting their answer to the equidistance property of circles.

periods.teacher_notes: The Square with Curves is the most demanding challenge here because students must reason that the arc's centre lies on the opposite side, not at the corner; if they are stuck, ask 'Where must the centre be so that the arc just touches both ends of the side it bulges from?' to guide them to the midpoint of the opposite side. Students who attempt all four challenges in one sitting should be encouraged to refine the precision of their earliest figure rather than rushing to a fifth.

textbook_segments.title: Exploring Diagonals of Rectangles and Squares

periods.activity_title: Measuring and Predicting Diagonal Properties

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Explore (diagonal bisects angles equally), section 8.5 p.204
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine how the rectangle must be constructed so that its diagonal divides the opposite angles into two equal parts.
Frame general laws observed about diagonal angles and side lengths; discuss whether these laws will always hold.

time_bands.activity: Students construct rectangle PQRS (sides of their choice), draw both diagonals PR and QS, and first predict — without measuring — whether the diagonals are equal, then measure to check. The class records results and begins to build the claim that the diagonals of a rectangle are equal.

Teacher introduces the labelling a–h for the eight angles formed by the two diagonals and the rectangle's sides. Students measure all eight angles and fill in a structured table, then mark which pairs are equal, building a data set for pattern recognition.

Explore (diagonal bisects angles equally), section 8.5 p.204 ("Determine how the rectangle must be constructed so that its diagonal divides the opposite angles into two equal parts….") — students reason from their table: when are the two angles at a corner made by the diagonal equal? They arrive at the condition that this requires the rectangle to be a square.

Math Talk (general laws), section 8.5 p.204 ("Frame general laws observed about diagonal angles and side lengths; discuss whether these laws will always hold….") — students draft one general law in their own words, then share with a partner to test whether the law is precise enough to apply to any rectangle.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly assume that diagonals of all quadrilaterals are equal; having them draw a non-rectangular parallelogram on the same sheet and measure its diagonals — if time permits — makes the rectangle's equal-diagonal property feel earned rather than given. Watch for incorrect angle labelling when the diagonals cross: ensure students label angles at the vertices of the rectangle, not at the intersection point.

textbook_segments.title: Exploring Diagonals of Rectangles and Squares

periods.activity_title: Constructing Rectangles from Diagonal Angle Conditions

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Construct (Rectangle with diagonal dividing angles 60°/30°), section 8.5 p.205
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a rectangle ABCD where diagonal AC divides angle A into 60° and 30°: draw AB, raise a 60° line from B to locate C, draw perpendicular through A, use compass or perpendicular from C to locate D, join to complete the rectangle.
Construct a rectangle in which one diagonal divides opposite angles into 50° and 40°.
Construct a rectangle in which one diagonal divides opposite angles into 45° and 45°; observe what this implies about the sides.

time_bands.activity: Construct (Rectangle with diagonal dividing angles 60°/30°), section 8.5 p.205 ("Construct a rectangle ABCD where diagonal AC divides angle A into 60° and 30°….") — teacher leads the construction step by step, asking students to predict at each stage which property (R1 or R2) is being enforced by the current step.

Construct Q1, section 8.5 p.211 ("Construct a rectangle in which one diagonal divides opposite angles into 50° and 40°….") — students work independently, applying the same method with new angle values; they verify the finished rectangle by measuring the second pair of opposite angles and checking that the same split appears.

Construct Q2, section 8.5 p.211 ("Construct a rectangle in which one diagonal divides opposite angles into 45° and 45°; observe what this implies about the sides….") — students construct the figure and measure the sides, arriving inductively at the conclusion that equal diagonal-angle splits imply equal sides, i.e., the rectangle is a square.

periods.teacher_notes: The key reasoning step here — that a 45°/45° split forces the rectangle to be a square — is best elicited by asking 'What does the diagonal do to the corner angle of a rectangle, and when would both halves be equal?' rather than stating it. A common error is using the wrong base angle when setting the 60° or 50° line; confirm that the angle is measured at the correct corner before the student proceeds.

textbook_segments.title: Exploring Diagonals of Rectangles and Squares

periods.activity_title: Constructing Rectangles from One Side and the Diagonal

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Construct (Rectangle, side 5 cm, diagonal 7 cm), section 8.5 p.208
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a rectangle with one side CD = 5 cm and diagonal BD = 7 cm: draw CD; raise perpendicular at C; draw circle of radius 7 cm centred at D; intersection with the perpendicular gives B; complete the rectangle.
Construct a rectangle with one side 4 cm and diagonal 8 cm.
Construct a rectangle with one side 3 cm and diagonal 7 cm.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the problem: 'You know one side and the diagonal of a rectangle — can you construct it?' Students attempt a rough sketch and identify which two properties of the rectangle and circle they would use, before the teacher walks through Construct (Rectangle, side 5 cm, diagonal 7 cm), section 8.5 p.208 ("draw CD; raise perpendicular at C; draw circle of radius 7 cm centred at D….") on the board.

Construct Q3, section 8.5 p.211 ("Construct a rectangle with one side 4 cm and diagonal 8 cm….") — students apply the method independently, then measure the second side and verify that the diagonals of the completed rectangle are equal.

Construct Q4, section 8.5 p.211 ("Construct a rectangle with one side 3 cm and diagonal 7 cm….") — students construct and compare the second side's length with that in Q3, noticing that the same diagonal length paired with different first sides produces rectangles with different proportions.

Students articulate in writing one sentence: 'The diagonal of a rectangle is always ___ than either side, because ___.' This formative writing consolidates the reasoning about the diagonal as the longest line segment in a rectangle.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes draw the circle arc on the wrong side of the perpendicular, placing B below the baseline; a quick check question — 'Should B be above or below CD if BCDA is to be a rectangle?' — corrects the orientation. For Construct Q3, a 4 cm side with an 8 cm diagonal produces a visually striking result that the diagonal is exactly twice the side, which sparks productive discussion about whether this is a coincidence.

textbook_segments.title: Points Equidistant from Two Given Points

periods.activity_title: Finding the Apex: Two Circles, One Intersection

textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a 'House' figure with all border lines 5 cm: draw base and walls; draw arcs of radius 5 cm centred at B and C; intersection gives apex A equidistant from both; draw arc of radius 5 cm from A to complete the curved roof.
Construct a bigger house in which all sides are of length 7 cm.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws two points B and C on the board (representing the top corners of a wall) and asks: 'Where is the set of all points exactly 5 cm from B?' Students recall the circle definition and answer: a circle of radius 5 cm centred at B. Teacher asks the same for C, then asks: 'Which point is on both circles at once?' — leading to the intersection idea.

Construct (House, sides 5 cm), section 8.6 p.211 ("Construct a 'House' figure with all border lines 5 cm: draw base and walls; draw arcs of radius 5 cm….") — teacher leads the full construction, drawing first full circles and then only the relevant arcs (Method 2), helping students see why arcs are more efficient than full circles.

Construct Q1, section 8.6 p.215 ("Construct a bigger house in which all sides are of length 7 cm….") — students apply the arc-intersection technique independently, then measure the two slant sides to confirm both equal 7 cm, verifying the equidistant-point property.
Students write a one-sentence answer: 'The apex A is equidistant from B and C because ___.', articulating why the arc-intersection guarantees equal distances rather than merely approximating them.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes draw only one arc and estimate the apex position by eye; insisting on two arcs and using their actual intersection point — even if it means re-drawing — establishes the geometric guarantee rather than a visual guess. The idea that all points on a circle are the same distance from the centre, established in section 8.1, is the direct foundation here.

textbook_segments.title: Points Equidistant from Two Given Points

periods.activity_title: Revisiting Artwork and the Rhombus Challenge

textbook_items_in_class.description: Recreate 'A Person', 'Wavy Wave', and 'Eyes' from section 8.1 using ideas from the House construction (equidistant-point technique).
Is there a 4-sided figure in which all sides are equal but is not a square? If so, construct it using the arc-intersection technique.

time_bands.activity: Construct Q2, section 8.6 p.215 ("Recreate 'A Person', 'Wavy Wave', and 'Eyes' from section 8.1 using ideas from the House construction….") — students choose one artwork figure and plan which centres and radii to use, explicitly applying the equidistant-point idea to place each arc centre so that the resulting curve is a precise circle or arc rather than a freehand estimate.

Construct Q3, section 8.6 p.215 ("Is there a 4-sided figure in which all sides are equal but is not a square? If so, construct it using the arc-intersection technique….") — students discuss whether such a figure exists, sketch a plan, then attempt construction using arc intersections to locate all four vertices with equal side lengths, discovering the rhombus.

Whole-class discussion: 'Does your figure have all four sides equal? Are all its angles 90°?' Students confirm the rhombus has equal sides but angles that are not necessarily 90°, clarifying the distinction from a square.

periods.teacher_notes: In Construct Q3, the common error is fixing all four angles at 90° out of habit, which produces a square rather than a rhombus; asking 'Does the problem require 90° angles?' before construction redirects students to the precise condition. The connection between Construct Q2 and section 8.1 is productive — students see that the artwork constructions they did intuitively earlier can now be reproduced with geometric guarantees.

textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw the rectangle-and-four-squares configuration on dot paper and describe what was done to place the four squares symmetrically around the rectangle.

time_bands.activity: Students plan an original composite artwork figure — choosing their own combination of circles, arcs, and rectangles — by sketching a rough diagram and annotating it with the centre positions, radii, and any square or rectangle dimensions they intend to use.

Figure it Out Q2, section 8.1 p.191 ("Take a central baseline of a different length and draw the wavy wave on it….") — students create a new wavy wave with a self-chosen baseline, integrating it into their planned artwork figure, adjusting compass settings to keep arcs uniform.

Figure it Out Q1, section 8.2 p.194 ("Draw the rectangle-and-four-squares configuration on dot paper and describe what was done to place the four squares symmetrically….") — students construct the configuration and write a description of their placement strategy, linking it to the equal-sides and right-angle properties of squares.

Students share their artwork sketch with a partner and identify one compass-and-ruler decision that they are confident about and one that required trial and adjustment, articulating the role of equidistance in each.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit deliberately revisits artwork and dot-grid work in a more open creative register; the aim is consolidation through play, so resist the temptation to over-direct. Students who struggle to start their own figure can use the 'A Person' figure from section 8.1 as a reference template and change one element.

Students review their two constructions for precision: do the inner square's corners lie exactly on the rectangle's sides? They note any adjustments needed and reflect on which construction step is most sensitive to compass inaccuracy.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is designed to build fluency through repetition of the full construction workflow without new content; the self-assessment step is therefore more important than speed — encourage students to measure carefully and record discrepancies honestly. A student whose rectangle is slightly off should be asked to identify which step introduced the error rather than simply redrawing from scratch.

periods.activity_title: Diagonal Laws: From Measurement to General Claim

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q (same-distance), section 8.4 p.199
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill the table for cases where X and Y are equidistant from A and B respectively; observe the resulting length XY and the shape of ABYX.
Frame general laws observed about diagonal angles and side lengths; discuss whether these laws will always hold.

time_bands.activity: Students construct two new rectangles with different proportions (teacher specifies two sets of dimensions on the board), draw both diagonals in each, label the eight angles a–h, and fill in the measurement table, building a richer data set than a single rectangle provides.

Figure it Out Q (same-distance), section 8.4 p.199 ("Fill the table for cases where X and Y are equidistant from A and B respectively; observe the resulting length XY and the shape of ABYX….") — students cross-check this result against their new rectangle data, verifying that the XY = AB result holds across different dimensions.

Math Talk (general laws), section 8.5 p.204 ("Frame general laws observed about diagonal angles and side lengths; discuss whether these laws will always hold….") — small groups pool their angle tables and formulate two general laws as written statements, then test each law against a classmate's rectangle to see whether it holds.

Each group states one law aloud. Teacher asks: 'How could you convince someone who has not measured anything that this law is always true?' — opening the door to reasoning beyond measurement, without requiring a formal proof.

periods.teacher_notes: The key pedagogical move here is the transition from 'it seems to be true for these cases' to 'here is a reason it must always be true'; keep the discussion at the level of verbal argument and spatial reasoning rather than algebra. Watch for groups who state a law too narrowly (e.g., only for a specific rectangle's dimensions) — prompt them to rewrite it without any numbers.

time_bands.activity: Construct Q1, section 8.5 p.211 ("Construct a rectangle in which one diagonal divides opposite angles into 50° and 40°….") — students use the diagonal-angle construction method, setting a 50° angle at the chosen corner, then apply the rectangle properties to complete the figure and verify that the opposite corners show the same 50°/40° split.

Construct Q2, section 8.5 p.211 ("Construct a rectangle in which one diagonal divides opposite angles into 45° and 45°; observe what this implies about the sides….") — students construct the figure and measure the sides, reasoning deductively that equal diagonal-angle splits at every corner force all four sides to be equal, making the figure a square.

Construct Q3, section 8.5 p.211 ("Construct a rectangle with one side 4 cm and diagonal 8 cm….") — students apply the perpendicular-and-circle method, locate the second vertex, complete the rectangle, and measure both diagonals to verify they are equal.

periods.teacher_notes: Construct Q2's result — that a 45°/45° diagonal split produces a square — is best treated as a discovery that students make by measuring, even though the deductive reasoning for it can be sketched verbally; do not simply announce it before construction. Construct Q3 with a 4 cm side and 8 cm diagonal produces a visually dramatic long rectangle that reinforces the idea that the diagonal is always longer than either side.

Construct Q3, section 8.6 p.215 ("Is there a 4-sided figure in which all sides are equal but is not a square? If so, construct it using the arc-intersection technique….") — students plan a rhombus construction on rough paper, apply the arc-intersection method to locate all four vertices, and measure all four sides and all four angles to characterise the resulting figure.

Discussion: 'Is the figure you constructed a square?' Students compare angle measurements and articulate the difference: a rhombus has all sides equal but its angles need not be 90°, while a square has both conditions. This establishes the rhombus as a distinct figure.

periods.teacher_notes: In the rhombus construction, students who happen to place their two base points such that the vertical distance equals the horizontal distance will construct a square; if this happens, ask them to redo the construction with a wider or narrower base to obtain a true rhombus. Measuring all four angles of the completed rhombus and noticing that opposite angles are equal — without being prompted — is a valuable extension observation worth drawing out in discussion.

time_bands.activity: Students choose their own measurements for the Shadings figure: outer square side, and the number and size of inner squares. They sketch a rough plan and annotate it with the dimensions, reasoning that each inner square's side must divide evenly into the outer square's side for the figure to tile exactly.

Construct Q3 (Shadings), section 8.4 p.202 ("Construct a shading figure — a square containing smaller squares — with measurements of own choice….") — students execute their planned figure with compass and ruler, using compass transfer to maintain equal spacing and equal side lengths for the inner squares.

Try This (Square with Curves), section 8.4 p.202 ("Construct a square of side 8 cm with four arcs bulging uniformly from each side; determine the correct centre placement….") — students reason that each arc's centre must be the midpoint of the opposite side and distance to the arc's reach must equal half the side length, then construct and verify symmetry by checking that all four arcs are congruent.
Students annotate their Square with Curves figure, labelling the four centres and the radius used, and write one sentence explaining why this placement guarantees symmetric arcs.

periods.teacher_notes: For Shadings, students who choose outer and inner squares with non-integer ratios will find the tiling does not close perfectly; this is a productive error — ask them to reason about what ratio is needed rather than simply adjusting by eye. For Square with Curves, students who place the arc centre at the corner rather than the midpoint of the opposite side produce asymmetric arcs; the self-check is to measure the arc's distance from each end of the side it bulges from.

periods.activity_title: The Compass Controls Distance: Four Problems, One Chapter
periods.teacher_notes: Refer to Prepared Table (see material: 'Problems and solutions') for the problems in full and their worked solutions. Pose all four problems on the board at once. Students work individually for the first half of the sitting, writing full construction steps or reasoning on paper. They then compare in groups of three: wherever answers differ, partners reconstruct each step aloud until the discrepancy is found. One student presents each problem; after each presentation the class names the chapter method used. Problem 1 needs the wavy-wave half-circle method — watch for students who use an incorrect radius or mis-place the centre of the second arc. Problem 2 needs the perpendicular-and-compass-transfer method for constructing a square — watch for students who mark the fourth vertex by eye instead of by compass swing. Problem 3 needs the diagonal-length construction method (perpendicular at one vertex, arc of given diagonal length) — watch for students who confuse the diagonal with the side. Problem 4 needs the arc-intersection equidistant-point method — watch for students who draw only one arc and guess the apex position.

visual_aids.title: Problems and solutions
visual_aids.table:
No. | Problem | Solution
1 | Draw a baseline PQ of 12 cm. On it construct a wavy wave made of three identical half-circles, each sitting on a 4 cm portion of PQ. What is the radius of each half-circle, and what are the centres of the three half-circles? | Each 4 cm portion has its midpoint as centre and radius 2 cm. Mark P, then points A (4 cm from P), B (8 cm from P), Q (12 cm from P). Centre of first half-circle: midpoint of PA = 2 cm from P; centre of second: midpoint of AB = 6 cm from P; centre of third: midpoint of BQ = 10 cm from P. Each arc has radius 2 cm. The three arcs, drawn alternately above and below PQ, form the wave.
2 | Construct square ABCD with side 5 cm. Use only a ruler and compass. Verify by measuring that BC = CD = DA = 5 cm. | Draw AB = 5 cm. At A, raise a perpendicular (by compass: mark two equal arcs from A on AB and beyond, bisect to get perpendicular direction). Mark D on the perpendicular 5 cm from A. At B, raise a perpendicular. Open compass to 5 cm; from D swing an arc; from B swing an arc of 5 cm; intersection is C. Join BC and DC. All four sides are 5 cm and all angles are 90°, confirming the square.
3 | Construct a rectangle with one side EF = 3 cm and diagonal EG = 7 cm. Label all four vertices. | Draw EF = 3 cm. At F raise a perpendicular. Open compass to 7 cm; place point at E; swing an arc cutting the perpendicular at G. FG is the adjacent side (= √(49 − 9) = √40 ≈ 6.3 cm, obtained by construction not calculation). From G drop a perpendicular to length EF; from E swing arc equal to FG to locate H. Join EH and GH. Rectangle EFGH has EF = 3 cm, diagonal EG = 7 cm, and both rectangle properties hold.
4 | Two points B and C are 6 cm apart. Find a point A that is exactly 6 cm from both B and C, and lies above BC. Then draw the triangle ABC. What kind of triangle is it? | Draw BC = 6 cm. Open compass to 6 cm; place point at B and draw an arc above BC. Keeping the same opening, place point at C and draw an arc above BC. The two arcs intersect at A. Draw AB and AC. By construction AB = AC = BC = 6 cm, so triangle ABC is equilateral — all three sides are 6 cm.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes all four problems on the board and reads each aloud. Students write the problems in their own space and confirm they have understood what is being asked before beginning. No hints are given; the board is the only reference.

Individual work: students attempt all four problems, writing full construction steps and showing every compass mark and reasoning line. They are expected to try each problem and return to earlier ones if they finish quickly. The teacher circulates silently, noting which problems are causing difficulty, but does not intervene.

Small-group comparison: groups of three compare answers problem by problem. Where any two students disagree on an answer or a step, they reconstruct that step aloud — 'I placed the compass here because…' — until the group reaches a shared, reasoned answer. The teacher listens in and notes groups who have resolved a disagreement correctly.

Whole-class presentations: one student presents each problem at the board, showing the key construction step or reasoning. After each presentation the class calls out the chapter method the solution rested on — half-circle arc placement, perpendicular-and-compass-transfer, diagonal-length arc, or arc-intersection for an equidistant point. The teacher affirms or corrects without elaborating beyond what the presenter could not supply.

Closing: the teacher states in one sentence the chapter's single idea — the compass fixes a distance exactly, and every construction in this chapter followed from placing that fixed distance in the right position — and the class is done.

items.prompt: A square has its four corners labelled P, Q, R, and S going around the figure in order. Which of the following is NOT a valid name for this square?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: PRSQ is not a valid name because it does not trace the corners in consecutive order around the square — it skips from P to R, missing Q.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A valid name for a square (or rectangle) must list corners in the order they appear when travelling around the figure, either clockwise or anticlockwise.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may not have checked whether PQRS is the canonical name; in fact it is valid because it traces the corners in order.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may believe that only names starting at a particular corner are valid; QRSP is valid because it starts at Q and goes around in the same direction.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may think that a name beginning at R is invalid; RSPQ is valid because it also traces consecutive corners in order.

inclusivity.support: Trace a finger around the square's corners in the order given by each name and check whether the finger returns to every corner exactly once without jumping.
inclusivity.challenge: Write down all possible valid names for the same square and explain the rule that generates them.

items.prompt: In rectangle ABCD, a point X lies on side AD and a point Y lies on side BC. When X is at a distance of 2 cm from A and Y is at a distance of 2 cm from B, what is the length of XY? Give a reason for your answer using the properties of a rectangle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: XY equals AB. Since X is 2 cm from A along AD and Y is 2 cm from B along BC, the two points are equidistant from their respective corners, making ABYX a rectangle with XY as one side opposite to AB. Because opposite sides of a rectangle are equal, XY = AB.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: When X and Y are equidistant from A and B respectively, ABYX is a rectangle and opposite-sides-equal (R1) gives XY = AB.

items.prompt: In rectangle ABCD with AB = 6 cm and BC = 4 cm, X is on AD and Y is on BC. A student claims that XY can never be longer than 6 cm. Is the student correct? Justify your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student is incorrect. The farthest distance between X and Y equals the diagonal of the rectangle, which is longer than either side. For a 6 cm × 4 cm rectangle the diagonal is √(36 + 16) = √52 ≈ 7.2 cm, which is greater than 6 cm. So XY can exceed 6 cm when X and Y are at opposite ends of the rectangle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The maximum XY equals the rectangle's diagonal, which is always longer than the longer side; measured via the Pythagorean relationship between sides and diagonal.

items.prompt: Priya draws a rectangle and measures its two diagonals. She finds they are equal. Her friend says this is just a coincidence for the rectangle Priya drew. Is the friend right? Explain why the diagonals of every rectangle must be equal, using the properties of a rectangle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The friend is wrong. In any rectangle PQRS, the two diagonals PR and QS connect opposite corners. Because all angles are 90° and opposite sides are equal (R1 and R2), the two triangles formed by each diagonal — for example triangle PQR and triangle QPS — share a common side PQ and have equal legs PQ and QR/PS. Both diagonals span the same two pairs of equal sides at right angles, so they must have the same length. This is not a coincidence but a consequence of the rectangle's properties.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the two rectangle properties (R1: opposite sides equal; R2: all angles 90°) to show the two triangles formed by each diagonal are congruent, making both diagonals equal.

inclusivity.support: Draw two different rectangles, measure both diagonals of each, and use the measurements to support your explanation.
inclusivity.challenge: Draw a parallelogram that is not a rectangle and measure its diagonals — explain why the equal-diagonal result does not hold there.

items.section_title: Exploring Diagonals of Rectangles and Squares
items.prompt: In rectangle ABCD, the diagonal AC divides angle A into two parts. A student measures these two parts and finds they are 35° and 55°. Another student says that without measuring, she can tell that the diagonal AC in any rectangle always divides angle A into two parts that add up to 90°. Explain why the second student's claim is always true, using what you know about rectangles.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: In rectangle ABCD, angle A is 90° (property R2: all angles of a rectangle are 90°). The diagonal AC lies inside the rectangle and meets at corner A. Whatever two angles it creates at A — call them angle BAC and angle DAC — they together must fill the full 90° corner. Since the whole corner at A is 90°, the two parts made by the diagonal must sum to 90° in every rectangle, regardless of the rectangle's side lengths.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Because every angle of a rectangle is 90° (R2), the diagonal splits that corner into two parts whose sum is always 90°.

inclusivity.support: Draw any rectangle, draw one diagonal, measure both angles it creates at one corner, and check whether they add up to 90°.
inclusivity.challenge: If the diagonal divides angle A into two equal parts of 45° each, what can you deduce about the sides of the rectangle? Justify your answer.

exercise.description: Construct a rectangle ABCD where diagonal AC divides angle A into 60° and 30°: draw AB, raise a 60° line from B to locate C, draw perpendicular through A, use compass or perpendicular from C to locate D, join to complete the rectangle.

items.section_title: Exploring Diagonals of Rectangles and Squares
items.prompt: A rectangle is to be constructed with one side of 5 cm and a diagonal of 7 cm. A student raises a perpendicular at one end of the 5 cm side and draws a circle of radius 7 cm centred at the other end. Explain why the intersection of this circle with the perpendicular gives the correct third corner of the rectangle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Call the 5 cm side CD. The perpendicular at C ensures that the angle at C is 90°, satisfying property R2. The circle of radius 7 cm centred at D gives all points at distance 7 cm from D — exactly the required diagonal length BD = 7 cm. The point B where the circle meets the perpendicular satisfies both conditions at once: it is at 90° from CD (the perpendicular) and at 7 cm from D (the circle). This double condition locates B precisely and correctly as the third corner.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The perpendicular enforces the 90° corner (R2); the circle of radius equal to the diagonal enforces the correct diagonal length; their intersection satisfies both simultaneously.

inclusivity.support: Try the construction with the given measurements, then measure angle B and diagonal BD of your completed rectangle to check.
inclusivity.challenge: What happens if the circle does not intersect the perpendicular at all? What does that tell you about the relationship between the side and the diagonal?

exercise.book_ref: Construct (Rectangle, side 5 cm, diagonal 7 cm), section 8.5 p.208
exercise.description: Construct a rectangle with one side CD = 5 cm and diagonal BD = 7 cm: draw CD; raise perpendicular at C; draw circle of radius 7 cm centred at D; intersection with the perpendicular gives B; complete the rectangle.

items.prompt: In rectangle ABCD (AB = 8 cm, BC = 5 cm), X is on AD and Y is on BC, both at a distance of 3 cm from A and B respectively. Rajan says ABYX is a rectangle. Is he right? Explain your answer using the properties of a rectangle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Rajan is right. Since X is 3 cm from A along AD and Y is 3 cm from B along BC, we have AX = BY = 3 cm. The side AB is perpendicular to both AD and BC (property R2). XY connects two points directly across the rectangle at equal distances from A and B, so XY is parallel to AB and equal in length to AB (= 8 cm). With AB = XY = 8 cm and AX = BY = 3 cm, ABYX has opposite sides equal and all angles 90°, satisfying both rectangle properties R1 and R2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Equal distances from A and B place X and Y symmetrically across the rectangle; R1 and R2 then confirm ABYX has opposite-sides-equal and all-angles-90°.

inclusivity.support: Draw the rectangle, mark X and Y, measure all four sides and all four angles of ABYX, and check the properties.
inclusivity.challenge: If X is 3 cm from A but Y is 4 cm from B, is ABYX still a rectangle? Explain.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q (same-distance), section 8.4 p.199
exercise.description: Fill the table for cases where X and Y are equidistant from A and B respectively; observe the resulting length XY and the shape of ABYX.

items.section_title: Exploring Diagonals of Rectangles and Squares
items.prompt: Rectangle ABCD is constructed so that diagonal AC divides angle A into 50° and 40°. Without constructing the rectangle, state the two angles into which diagonal AC divides angle C. Give a reason.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Diagonal AC divides angle C into 50° and 40° as well. Angle A and angle C are opposite corners of the rectangle, and the diagonal AC connects them. The two triangles ABC and CDA formed by the diagonal are congruent (same side lengths, right angles at B and D). Therefore the diagonal makes the same pair of angles at C as it does at A — that is, 50° and 40° at C also.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Opposite corners of a rectangle are mirror images across the diagonal; congruent triangles formed by the diagonal guarantee the same angle split at both ends.

inclusivity.support: Construct the rectangle, draw the diagonal, and measure the angles at C to check.
inclusivity.challenge: What angles does the diagonal make at corners B and D? Explain whether these are the same as at A and C or different.

exercise.book_ref: Construct Q1, section 8.5 p.211
exercise.description: Construct a rectangle in which one diagonal divides opposite angles into 50° and 40°.

items.prompt: A student wants to draw a circle such that every point on the circle is exactly 3 cm from a fixed point P. To what length should the student open the compass? If the student instead opens the compass to 5 cm from the same point P and draws a second circle, what is the distance between the two circles measured along a straight line from P?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The compass should be opened to 3 cm, because every point on a circle is at a distance equal to the radius from the centre. The first circle has radius 3 cm and the second has radius 5 cm, both centred at P. Along any straight line from P, the first circle is reached at 3 cm and the second at 5 cm, so the gap between the two circles along that line is 5 − 3 = 2 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the definition that the compass opening equals the radius; subtract the two radii to find the gap between concentric circles along a radius line.

inclusivity.support: Draw both circles on paper with a compass, then use a ruler to measure the gap between them along a line from P.
inclusivity.challenge: If a third circle is drawn from P so that the gap between the second and third circles is also 2 cm, what is the radius of the third circle?

exercise.book_ref: Activity (compass exploration), section 8.1 p.188
exercise.description: Students mark a point P, then use a compass set to 4 cm to trace all points 4 cm from P, discovering that the resulting curve is a circle with centre P and radius 4 cm.

items.prompt: A wavy wave is to be drawn on a baseline of 12 cm using identical half-circles placed side by side. Each half-circle's diameter spans one equal portion of the baseline. If the wave has 3 half-circles, what is the radius of each half-circle? What should be the length AX (the first segment of the baseline from point A to the first half-circle's centre)?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: With 3 identical half-circles on a 12 cm baseline, each half-circle spans 12 ÷ 3 = 4 cm of the baseline, so each half-circle has diameter 4 cm and radius 2 cm. The first half-circle is centred at the midpoint of the first 4 cm segment, so AX = 2 cm (half of 4 cm, from A to the first centre).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the baseline equally among the half-circles to find each diameter; halve the diameter for the radius; halve the first segment length for AX.

inclusivity.support: Draw a 12 cm baseline and mark it into 3 equal parts of 4 cm each, then identify the midpoint of the first part as the first centre.
inclusivity.challenge: If the same 12 cm baseline is used with 4 identical half-circles instead of 3, recalculate the radius and AX, and compare the appearance of the two waves.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 8.1 p.191
exercise.description: What radius should be taken in the compass to draw the first half-circle of the Wavy Wave? What should be the length of AX?

items.prompt: A square PQRS has a side of 5 cm. After constructing the square using ruler and compass, a student measures the diagonal PR. What is the length of PR to one decimal place? Also state which two rectangle or square properties guarantee that the construction produces a square and not just any quadrilateral.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The diagonal PR = √(5² + 5²) = √50 ≈ 7.1 cm (to one decimal place). The two properties that guarantee the construction produces a square are S1 (all four sides equal, each 5 cm) and S2 (all four angles equal 90°).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the Pythagorean relationship to find the diagonal of a square (diagonal = side × √2); cite S1 and S2 as the defining properties.

inclusivity.support: Construct the square, measure PR with a ruler, and compare the measurement with √50.
inclusivity.challenge: If a rectangle has sides 5 cm and 8 cm, calculate its diagonal to one decimal place and compare with the square's diagonal.

exercise.book_ref: Construct (Square PQRS, 6 cm), section 8.3 p.195
exercise.description: Six-step construction of square PQRS with side 6 cm: draw PQ; raise perpendicular at P; mark S at 6 cm on perpendicular; raise perpendicular at Q; use compass to mark R at 6 cm from both S and Q; join to complete.

items.prompt: A student constructs a rectangle with sides 2 cm and 10 cm. After construction, she checks both rectangle properties. (a) What are the lengths of all four sides? (b) What is the size of each interior angle?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Two sides are 2 cm each and two sides are 10 cm each, because property R1 states that opposite sides of a rectangle are equal. (b) Each interior angle is 90°, because property R2 states that all angles of a rectangle are 90°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read off both rectangle properties directly: R1 gives opposite-sides-equal, R2 gives all-angles-90°.

inclusivity.support: Construct the rectangle and use a ruler and protractor to measure and record all four sides and all four angles.
inclusivity.challenge: Calculate the length of the diagonal of this rectangle to one decimal place and explain whether a rectangle with these dimensions can be divided into identical squares.

exercise.book_ref: Construct Q2, section 8.3 p.197
exercise.description: Draw a rectangle with sides 2 cm and 10 cm and verify it satisfies both rectangle properties.

items.prompt: A student uses the compass length-transfer technique to construct a rectangle that can be divided into exactly two identical squares. She chooses a breadth of 4 cm. (a) What length must the rectangle have? (b) After construction, she wants to verify the division by drawing a line parallel to the shorter sides at the midpoint. How far from each short side should this line be drawn?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) The length must be 8 cm, because a rectangle divides into two identical squares when its length equals twice its breadth (2 × 4 = 8 cm). (b) The dividing line should be drawn 4 cm from each short side (at the midpoint of the 8 cm length), since each of the two squares has side 4 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the two-identical-squares condition (length = 2 × breadth) to find the length; halve the length for the position of the dividing line.

inclusivity.support: Draw a 4 cm × 8 cm rectangle and physically fold it in half along the longer dimension to check the two squares.
inclusivity.challenge: If the same technique is applied to make a rectangle divisible into three identical squares with breadth 4 cm, what is the new length and where are the two dividing lines drawn?

exercise.book_ref: Construct (Breaking Rectangles — two squares), section 8.4 p.200
exercise.description: Plan and construct a rectangle divisible into two identical squares: set AF to any chosen length, transfer AF using compass to mark B at AB = AF, raise perpendicular at B, mark C at BC = AF, join to complete rectangle ACDF.

items.prompt: A rectangle is to be divided into exactly three identical squares. If each square has a side of 3 cm, what are the dimensions of the rectangle?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each square has a side of 3 cm. When three squares are placed side by side along the length, the rectangle's length = 3 × 3 = 9 cm and its breadth = 3 cm. So the rectangle is 9 cm × 3 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the square's side by 3 to find the length; the breadth equals the square's side.

inclusivity.support: Sketch three squares of side 3 cm placed in a row and measure the total width.
inclusivity.challenge: Give two different sets of rectangle dimensions (other than 9 cm × 3 cm) that can each be divided into three identical squares, and state the side length of the squares in each case.

exercise.book_ref: Construct (Breaking Rectangles — three squares), section 8.4 p.199
exercise.description: Construct a rectangle that can be divided into three identical squares.

items.prompt: A square of side 8 cm is to contain a smaller square whose centre coincides with the centre of the larger square. The smaller square's side is 4 cm. How far is each corner of the smaller square from each side of the larger square?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The larger square has side 8 cm and the smaller has side 4 cm. The smaller square is centred inside the larger one, so the gap on each side between the smaller square's edge and the larger square's edge is (8 − 4) ÷ 2 = 2 cm. Each corner of the smaller square is therefore 2 cm from the nearest side of the larger square.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the inner square's side from the outer square's side and halve the difference to find the uniform gap on each side.

inclusivity.support: Draw both squares on squared paper with the inner square centred, and measure the gap on one side.
inclusivity.challenge: If the inner square's side were 6 cm instead of 4 cm, what would the new gap be, and would the corners of the inner square still fit inside the outer square?

exercise.book_ref: Construct Q1 (Square within Rectangle), section 8.4 p.201
exercise.description: Construct a rectangle of sides 8 cm and 4 cm, then construct a square inside it such that the centre of the square coincides with the centre of the rectangle.

items.prompt: A square of side 8 cm has four arcs, one bulging out from the centre of each side. Each arc is drawn using the midpoint of the opposite side as the compass centre. If the compass is set so that the arc just reaches the two corners of the side it bulges from, what is the radius used for each arc?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each arc is centred at the midpoint of the opposite side. The distance from this midpoint to one corner of the side the arc bulges from equals the distance from the midpoint of one side to the far corner of the opposite side. The midpoint of a side is 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cm from each end of that side. The distance from that midpoint to the far corner combines the full side length of 8 cm across the square and half the opposite side length of 4 cm, giving √(8² + 4²) = √(64 + 16) = √80 ≈ 8.9 cm. However, the arc only needs to reach the two ends of the side it bulges from: the distance from the midpoint of the opposite side to one corner of the bulging side is √(8² + 4²) = √80 ≈ 8.9 cm. So the radius is √80 ≈ 8.9 cm (approximately 8.9 cm).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the distance from the midpoint of one side to a corner of the opposite side using the Pythagorean relationship: √(side² + (side/2)²).

inclusivity.support: Draw the 8 cm square, mark the midpoint of one side, draw a line to one corner of the opposite side, and measure that line with a ruler.
inclusivity.challenge: If the square's side were 6 cm instead of 8 cm, recalculate the radius needed and compare the two results.

exercise.book_ref: Try This (Square with Curves), section 8.4 p.202
exercise.description: Construct a square of side 8 cm with four arcs bulging uniformly from each side; determine the correct centre placement for the compass to produce symmetric arcs.

items.section_title: Points Equidistant from Two Given Points
items.prompt: Two points B and C are 6 cm apart. A student draws arcs of radius 6 cm centred at B and at C. (a) How many intersection points will the two arcs have (above the line BC)? (b) If the intersection point above BC is called A, what are the lengths AB and AC?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) The two arcs of equal radius 6 cm centred at points 6 cm apart will intersect at exactly one point above BC (and one below). (b) A is on the arc of radius 6 cm from B, so AB = 6 cm. A is also on the arc of radius 6 cm from C, so AC = 6 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Each arc is the locus of points at radius 6 cm from its centre; the intersection point lies on both arcs, so both distances equal 6 cm.

inclusivity.support: Draw the two arcs with a compass and ruler and measure AB and AC on your drawing.
inclusivity.challenge: What kind of triangle is ABC? Give a reason using the three side lengths.

items.section_title: Points Equidistant from Two Given Points
items.prompt: A house figure is to be constructed with all straight sides equal to 7 cm. The rectangular base has width 7 cm. Two arcs of radius 7 cm are drawn from the two top corners of the walls to locate the apex. How far above the midpoint of the top wall is the apex? (Give your answer to one decimal place.)

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The two top corners B and C are 7 cm apart (the width of the wall). The apex A is located by the intersection of arcs of radius 7 cm from B and from C. Triangle ABC has AB = AC = BC = 7 cm, making it equilateral. The height of an equilateral triangle with side 7 cm is (√3 / 2) × 7 = (1.732 / 2) × 7 ≈ 0.866 × 7 ≈ 6.1 cm. So the apex is approximately 6.1 cm above the midpoint of the top wall.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Triangle ABC with AB = AC = BC = 7 cm is equilateral; its height = (√3/2) × 7 ≈ 6.1 cm.

inclusivity.support: Construct the house with all sides 7 cm and measure the height of the apex above the top wall with a ruler.
inclusivity.challenge: If all sides were 5 cm instead of 7 cm, calculate the height of the apex above the top wall and compare the two houses.

exercise.book_ref: Construct Q1, section 8.6 p.215
exercise.description: Construct a bigger house in which all sides are of length 7 cm.

items.prompt: A student draws a wavy wave on a baseline of 16 cm using 4 identical half-circles. What is the radius of each half-circle? If a second student draws the same wave but uses 8 identical half-circles on the same 16 cm baseline, what is the radius of each of the second student's half-circles?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: For 4 half-circles on 16 cm: each half-circle spans 16 ÷ 4 = 4 cm, so diameter = 4 cm and radius = 2 cm. For 8 half-circles on 16 cm: each spans 16 ÷ 8 = 2 cm, so diameter = 2 cm and radius = 1 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the baseline by the number of half-circles to get each diameter; halve to get the radius.

inclusivity.support: Mark the 16 cm baseline into 4 equal parts, identify the midpoint of the first part, and measure it to confirm the radius.
inclusivity.challenge: How many half-circles would give a radius of 0.5 cm on the same 16 cm baseline, and what would the wave look like compared to the 4-half-circle version?

exercise.description: Take a central baseline of a different length and draw the wavy wave on it.

items.prompt: A student constructs a rectangle with sides 4 cm and 6 cm. After finishing, she checks property R1 by measuring the opposite sides and property R2 by measuring one angle. (a) What measurement should she record for each pair of opposite sides? (b) What angle should she record for property R2?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) One pair of opposite sides should each measure 4 cm and the other pair should each measure 6 cm, confirming R1 (opposite sides equal). (b) The angle should be 90°, confirming R2 (all angles of a rectangle are 90°).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply R1 (opposite sides equal) and R2 (all angles 90°) directly to the given dimensions.

inclusivity.support: Construct the rectangle and use a ruler and protractor to record all four side lengths and one corner angle.
inclusivity.challenge: Calculate the length of the diagonal of this 4 cm × 6 cm rectangle to one decimal place.

items.prompt: A square of side 8 cm is to be decorated with four identical arcs, one on each side, each bulging outward from the centre of its side. A student places the compass centre at the midpoint of the opposite side and draws the arc so that it passes through the two corners of the side it belongs to. Explain in one or two sentences why placing the compass centre at the midpoint of the opposite side — rather than at any other point — guarantees that all four arcs are identical.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The midpoint of the opposite side is the same distance from both corners of the arc's side, so the arc is symmetric about the midpoint of its own side. Because all four sides of a square are equal and all four midpoints are positioned in the same way relative to the opposite side, every arc has the same radius and the same symmetric shape, making all four arcs identical.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The midpoint of the opposite side is equidistant from both ends of the arc's side; equal sides of the square mean all four midpoints produce identical radii and identical arcs.

inclusivity.support: Measure the distance from the midpoint of one side to each of the two corners of the opposite side and check that the two distances are equal.
inclusivity.challenge: If the compass centre were placed at a point one-quarter of the way along the opposite side instead of at the midpoint, would the arc still be symmetric? Explain.

items.section_title: Exploring Diagonals of Rectangles and Squares
items.prompt: A rectangle is constructed with one side of 3 cm and a diagonal of 7 cm. After construction, a student measures the other side. Using the relationship between sides and diagonal of a rectangle, calculate the length of the other side to one decimal place.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: In a rectangle, the diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle formed by the two sides. With one side = 3 cm and diagonal = 7 cm, the other side = √(7² − 3²) = √(49 − 9) = √40 ≈ 6.3 cm (to one decimal place).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the Pythagorean relationship: other side = √(diagonal² − known side²) = √(49 − 9) = √40 ≈ 6.3 cm.

inclusivity.support: Construct the rectangle using the perpendicular-and-circle method, then measure the second side directly with a ruler.
inclusivity.challenge: Construct a rectangle with one side 3 cm and diagonal 7 cm, draw both diagonals, and measure all eight angles formed at the two ends of one diagonal.

exercise.description: Construct a rectangle with one side 3 cm and diagonal 7 cm.

items.section_title: Points Equidistant from Two Given Points
items.prompt: A designer wants to construct a four-sided figure in which all four sides are equal but the angles are not all 90°. Describe, in two or three sentences, how the arc-intersection technique can be used to locate all four vertices of such a figure, and name the figure produced.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Draw a base segment AB of the chosen side length. To find vertex D such that AD equals AB, draw an arc of radius AB centred at A; D can be any point on this arc other than B. To find vertex C such that BC = CD = AB, draw an arc of radius AB centred at B and an arc of radius AB centred at D; their intersection gives C. Joining A, B, C, D produces a four-sided figure with all sides equal but with angles that depend on the chosen position of D — this figure is a rhombus.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use arc-intersection to locate each vertex at the required equal distance from two already-placed vertices; the resulting figure with all sides equal but not necessarily 90° angles is a rhombus.

inclusivity.support: Refer to the House construction method: just as the apex was found by intersecting two arcs, use the same idea to locate each new vertex of the rhombus.
inclusivity.challenge: Construct a rhombus with all sides 5 cm and measure all four angles; describe the relationship between opposite angles.

exercise.book_ref: Construct Q3, section 8.6 p.215
exercise.description: Is there a 4-sided figure in which all sides are equal but is not a square? If so, construct it using the arc-intersection technique.

items.section_title: Points Equidistant from Two Given Points
items.prompt: In the Artwork constructions, the 'Eyes' figure uses two arcs to form each eye. If each arc is drawn with a radius of 3 cm and the two arcs forming one eye are centred at two points P and Q that are 4 cm apart, and both arcs pass through the same two intersection points, how far is each intersection point from the line PQ? (Give your answer to one decimal place.)

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each arc has radius 3 cm and the centres P and Q are 4 cm apart. The intersection points lie on both circles. The midpoint M of PQ is 2 cm from each centre. For intersection point A: AM² = PA² − PM² = 3² − 2² = 9 − 4 = 5, so AM = √5 ≈ 2.2 cm. Each intersection point is approximately 2.2 cm from the line PQ.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the Pythagorean relationship in the right triangle formed by the half-distance between centres, the radius, and the perpendicular height to the line PQ.

inclusivity.support: Draw the two circles with a compass, mark the two intersection points, and measure their distance from line PQ with a ruler.
inclusivity.challenge: If the two centres were 5 cm apart instead of 4 cm, would the circles still intersect? Calculate the distance between intersection points and compare.
